idiom_name: id-to-lambda hash + cursor loop; Enumerable#inject for the pure fold
implementation_notes: Ruby expresses the itinerary as a hash of step id -> lambda (or proc) plus a cursor on a plain hash envelope, applied with a while loop or each; Enumerable#inject/reduce folds a pure chain into one transformation, and Proc#>> composes two steps, so the classic Router/Step class structure is replaced by procs. Rack's middleware stack (use Middleware(...) wrapping the next app) is the ecosystem's canonical chain, but its order is fixed when the app is built, which makes it a cousin of the pattern rather than an implementation. Sidekiq/ActiveJob style background jobs should carry the step id and cursor in their payload and re-enqueue the next step, since procs cannot be serialised.
code_sketch:
SLIP = { "validate" => ->(m) { validate(m) }, "reserve" => ->(m) { reserve(m) },
         "charge" => ->(m) { charge(m) } }

def advance(env)
  while env[:cursor] < env[:slip].length
    step = SLIP.fetch(env[:slip][env[:cursor]])
    env[:body] = step.call(env[:body])
    env[:cursor] += 1
  end
  env
end
pitfalls: inject/reduce keeps no progress state, so a mid-chain exception loses how far the message got - use an explicit cursor when retries must resume.
Procs and hashes with symbol keys are not broker-serialisable: Sidekiq/Resque payloads must carry step ids and the cursor, not the lambdas.
Procs in a threaded server (Puma) capture per-request objects; a slip stored on the class or in a constant keeps them alive and leaks memory.
Fetching with [] silently yields nil for an unknown step and blows up with NoMethodError far from the cause - use fetch or an explicit unknown-step error.
